rationale: B wins by a nose because it gives the founder four genuinely different doors into the story, especially the serviceable reader angle, "What Rivian's charger opening actually means for non-Rivian EV owners — and what they'll pay for it." A is cleaner on facts, but "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates — the loyalty math of a shared network" is mostly the same premium-pricing fact wearing a customer-retention hat. B still needs its Tesla language muzzled; "fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" is too cocky for the supplied facts.
gaps_in_A: "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates — the loyalty math of a shared network" duplicates "Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more than its own"; same pricing fact, new wrapper.
"the way it has for one walled competitor" sneaks in an unsupported competitor analogy; source it or cut it.
It misses the most practical service angle for non-Rivian drivers: app access, compatible cars/connectors, and the actual premium.
"NACS-standardization context is current" needs a real outside peg or it stays a generic trend label.
gaps_in_B: "Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" overstates the supplied facts; no Rivian competitive positioning or Tesla comparison was provided.
"following the industry's shift away from automaker-exclusive plugs" is a market thesis, not a fact in the update; it needs sourcing before it can carry a headline.
"newest brand-agnostic fast-charging grid" is a little grand for 3,500+ chargers without scale context; prove the network is big enough to matter.
The next step jumps to `find-journalists` before the missing price delta, compatibility details, and scale comparison are nailed down; list-building on thin proof is just organized spam.
